# Image Optimization Techniques (Hero Component)

Notes from converting `cleanmax-reference/sections/hero.liquid` to `components/Hero.tsx`. For study only.

## 1. Next's image optimizer, via `getImageProps()` — not the `<Image>` component

**What:** The final markup in `Hero.tsx` is a plain `<img>` tag (see #2 for why), but its `src`/`srcSet` are generated by `getImageProps()`, which runs the *same* optimization pipeline as the `<Image>` component — it's the function form of the same loader/config, not a separate lighter-weight path.

**Why:** Next.js's image optimizer resizes, re-encodes, and serves images on demand instead of shipping whatever fixed file the CMS/CDN provides. We need that pipeline's *output* (the optimized URLs), but we need to place the result inside a hand-built `<picture>` element (#2), which the `<Image>` component doesn't support directly.

**Improvement:**
- Automatic modern format negotiation (AVIF/WebP) based on the browser's `Accept` header — smaller file size than the source PNG/JPEG.
- Automatic `srcSet` generation across multiple widths, so a phone downloads a phone-sized image instead of the same 2000px desktop file.

**What we give up by not rendering `<Image>` directly:** its automatic `loading="lazy"`/IntersectionObserver wiring (moot here since the hero forces `priority`, see #3) and its automatic inline aspect-ratio styling (moot here since the layout already reserves space via #5). Everything about the actual image bytes/URLs is unaffected.

## 2. `getImageProps()` + real `<picture>`/`<source>` ("Art Direction" pattern)

**What:** Instead of rendering two `<Image>` components and hiding one with CSS (`hidden md:block`), we call `getImageProps()` to get the optimized `srcSet` for each image, then hand-assemble a native `<picture>` element with `<source media="...">` + fallback `<img>`.

**Why:** A hero often needs a completely different crop/image for mobile vs. desktop (not just a smaller version of the same image) — that's "art direction," and `next/image` has no built-in `<picture>` support.

**The trap we avoided:** Our first attempt rendered *both* `<Image>` components in the DOM and toggled visibility with Tailwind's `hidden`/`md:block` classes. Because the hero is above the fold, both images needed `priority` (eager loading) for good LCP — but `priority` forces the browser to fetch the image immediately **regardless of its CSS display state**. Result: both the mobile and desktop image downloaded on every page load, wasting bandwidth on exactly the assets we were trying to optimize.

**Improvement:**
- The browser's native `<picture>` element evaluates the `media` query *before* fetching, so only one image (mobile or desktop) is ever requested — restoring the "single download" behavior the old Liquid `<picture>` markup already had.
- Each candidate image (`desktop`, `mobile`) still runs through Next's optimizer via `getImageProps()`, so we keep the responsive `srcSet` + format conversion from #1.
- Net result: same optimization benefits as `next/image`, with the request efficiency of native `<picture>` — best of both approaches.

## 3. `priority` + `fetchPriority="high"` on hero images

**What:** Set on both the desktop and mobile `getImageProps()` calls.

**Why:** The hero image is almost always the page's Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) element. Next's default lazy-loading (`loading="lazy"`) would delay it until the browser decides it's near the viewport — actively hurting the LCP metric for content that's already visible on load.

**Improvement:** `priority` disables lazy-loading and preloads the image; `fetchPriority="high"` tells the browser's network stack to fetch it before lower-priority resources (fonts, below-the-fold images, scripts). Together they push LCP as early as possible.

## 4. Explicit `width`/`height` on every image

**What:** Every `getImageProps()`/`<Image>` call passes `width` and `height` (or `fill`), never lets them default.

**Why:** Next.js uses these to reserve the correct aspect ratio in the layout *before* the image loads.

**Improvement:** Prevents Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) — the page doesn't jump/reflow when the image finishes downloading, because the browser already reserved the right amount of space.

## 5. Aspect-ratio container instead of relying on image dimensions

**What:** The image wrapper uses `pb-[75%]` (padding-bottom trick) on mobile and a fixed `md:h-[650px]` on desktop, with the image absolutely positioned inside (`absolute inset-0 h-full w-full object-cover`).

**Why:** The real image dimensions aren't known at build time (they come from a remote CDN/CMS), and the mobile/desktop crops have different aspect ratios.

**Improvement:** The layout box is stable and correct on first paint regardless of the actual source image's dimensions, avoiding CLS while still allowing `object-cover` to crop the image to fill the box without distortion.

## 6. `remotePatterns` allowlist in `next.config.ts`

**What:** Restricted optimizable remote images to `https://cleanmax.com.ar/cdn/shop/**` instead of allowing any external host.

**Why:** Next.js requires you to explicitly allow-list remote image hosts before it will optimize them — this is a security control, not a formatting requirement.

**Improvement:** Prevents the image optimizer from being used as an open proxy/SSRF vector for arbitrary attacker-supplied URLs, while still being scoped narrowly enough (protocol + host + path prefix) to only cover the CDN paths we actually use.

## 7. `sizes="100vw"` on full-bleed images

**What:** Told the browser the image will render at 100% of the viewport width.

**Why:** Without `sizes`, the browser can't know how large the image will actually be rendered, and Next.js/the browser fall back to conservative assumptions that can pick a larger-than-needed candidate from the `srcSet`.

**Improvement:** The browser downloads the `srcSet` candidate that actually matches the rendered width, instead of over-fetching.

## 8. Props-driven, no baked-in content

**What:** All merchant-editable fields (`bgColor`, `imageDesktop`, `imageMobile`, `title`, `description`, `btnLabel`, `btnLink`) are required component props with no defaults; the calling page supplies real values.

**Why:** Not a performance technique on its own, but it's what makes the optimizations above swappable later — when this section is wired to WooCommerce, the same `getImageProps()`/`<picture>` logic keeps working no matter what URLs/copy come back from the API.

**Improvement:** Decouples "how images are optimized" from "where the data comes from," so future data-fetching work doesn't require touching the optimization logic.

## 9. Static `import` for local images (Header logo)

**What:** In `components/Header.tsx`, the logo is loaded with `import Logo from "@/public/clean-max-logo.png"` and passed straight to `<Image src={Logo} .../>`, instead of writing `src="/clean-max-logo.png"` as a string.

**Why:** The source file was a 1MB PNG. A string `src` still gets optimized by Next, but Next has to guess/require manual `width`/`height`, and can't generate a `blurDataURL` on its own. A static `import` reads the file at build time, so Next already knows its exact intrinsic width/height and can auto-generate a base64 blur placeholder — no manual guessing.

**Improvement:**
- Same resize/format-negotiation pipeline as the remote hero images (#1), so the 1MB source is served as a handful of KB at the ~80–96px display size actually used.
- `placeholder="blur"` works for free (no extra props needed) — the tiny blurred preview paints instantly while the optimized image loads, instead of a blank gap.
- No `next.config.ts` allow-listing needed (unlike remote images, #6) — local files under `public/` don't go through the SSRF-risk remote-image path at all.
